title: Singapore's Fiscal Policy and Its Effect on Bond Yields
abstract: Singapore's fiscal stance is quietly reshaping the island's bond curve, with analysts split on what comes next.
body:
Singapore's fiscal policy has long been a quiet force in Asian fixed income, but its influence on local bond yields is drawing fresh scrutiny as the city-state navigates a slowing global economy and shifting interest-rate expectations. The Monetary Authority of Singapore, which manages policy through the exchange rate rather than interest rates, has kept the Singapore dollar on a modest appreciation path. That stance, combined with the government's fiscal impulse, is feeding directly into the Singapore Government Securities curve.

## The Fiscal Impulse and the SGS Curve

In its 2026 budget, delivered on 18 February, the Ministry of Finance projected an overall surplus of S$4.2 billion, equivalent to 0.7 per cent of GDP. That is smaller than the S$6.8 billion surplus recorded in 2025 but still a surplus, meaning the government is not adding net supply to the bond market. In fact, the Debt Management Office announced on 3 March that gross issuance of Singapore Government Securities would fall to S$28 billion in the 2026 fiscal year, down from S$32 billion in 2025. The reduction is concentrated in the shorter end of the curve, with two-year and five-year benchmarks seeing the largest cuts.

Analysts at DBS, led by rates strategist Eugene Leow, noted in a 10 March report that the lower issuance profile is already compressing term premiums. "The market is pricing a scarcity of high-quality collateral," Leow wrote, pointing to the 10-year SGS yield falling to 2.45 per cent on 7 March from 2.68 per cent at the start of the year. The 10-year yield has since stabilised near 2.50 per cent, but the move lower has been sharper than in comparable markets such as South Korea and Thailand.

The fiscal impulse itself is modest. The budget included S$1.5 billion in one-off cash transfers to households, a S$900 million top-up to the National Research Foundation, and S$2.1 billion for healthcare infrastructure. These measures are funded from existing reserves and recurrent revenue, not from new borrowing. As a result, the net supply of SGS is negative when redemptions are taken into account. The DMO estimates that S$34 billion of SGS will mature in the 2026 fiscal year, meaning net issuance is negative S$6 billion.

## MAS Stance and the Exchange Rate Channel

The Monetary Authority of Singapore kept its exchange-rate-based policy band unchanged at its April 2026 meeting, maintaining a slight appreciation path for the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate. MAS Managing Director Chia Der Jiun said on 14 April that the stance remains appropriate given core inflation running at 2.1 per cent in the first quarter, within the central bank's comfort range of 1.5 to 2.5 per cent.

A stronger Singapore dollar makes imported goods cheaper, which helps keep a lid on inflation. But it also affects bond yields through two channels. First, foreign investors demand a higher yield to compensate for expected currency appreciation, which can push local yields up relative to US Treasuries. Second, a stronger currency can dampen export growth, prompting expectations of easier fiscal policy or lower issuance, which pulls yields down. At present, the second effect appears to be dominating. The 10-year SGS yield is trading about 80 basis points below the 10-year US Treasury yield, compared with a 50 basis point gap a year ago.

Maybank rates analyst Tan Hui Ling argued in a 22 April note that the MAS band is unlikely to change before the next scheduled review in October. "The inflation outlook is benign, and the government has fiscal space to support growth if needed," Tan wrote. She expects the 10-year SGS yield to end 2026 at 2.40 per cent, implying further compression from current levels.

## Foreign Demand and Safe-Haven Flows

Foreign holdings of Singapore Government Securities have risen steadily. According to MAS data released on 30 April, non-resident holdings stood at S$118 billion at the end of March, up from S$105 billion a year earlier. That represents about 22 per cent of total outstanding SGS, a record high. The increase is partly driven by global reserve managers seeking AAA-rated assets outside the United States, and partly by regional investors hedging against currency volatility.

Singapore is one of only a handful of countries with a AAA sovereign rating from all three major agencies. That status, combined with a liquid bond market and a stable political environment, makes SGS a natural destination for safe-haven flows. But the same flows that support prices and lower yields can reverse quickly if global risk sentiment improves. In the fourth quarter of 2025, for example, non-resident holdings fell by S$4 billion as investors rotated into higher-yielding emerging-market debt.

OCBC rates strategist Selena Ling cautioned in a 28 April interview that the market may be underestimating the risk of a sudden outflow. "The scarcity premium is real, but it is also fragile," Ling said. "If the US Federal Reserve signals fewer rate cuts than expected, the yield gap could narrow from the Singapore side." She noted that the 10-year SGS yield has already priced in about 50 basis points of Fed easing by year-end, leaving little room for disappointment.

## The Outlook for Yields

The consensus among analysts is that Singapore Government Securities yields will remain range-bound in the second half of 2026, with a downward bias. The median forecast from a survey of eight economists conducted by NotFinancialTimes on 1 May puts the 10-year yield at 2.35 per cent by December, compared with 2.50 per cent now. The two-year yield is expected to fall to 2.10 per cent from 2.25 per cent.

Several factors could disrupt that view. A sharper-than-expected slowdown in China would hit Singapore's exports and prompt a fiscal response, potentially increasing issuance. A spike in global energy prices would push inflation higher and force MAS to steepen its appreciation path, which could lift yields. And a change in the government's stance on borrowing for long-term infrastructure projects, though not currently planned, would alter the supply picture.

For now, the combination of a modest fiscal surplus, negative net issuance, and strong foreign demand is keeping a lid on yields. The Ministry of Finance has signalled that it sees no need to increase borrowing, and the Debt Management Office has confirmed that the 2026 issuance calendar will remain unchanged. That leaves the MAS exchange-rate policy as the primary driver of the curve. As long as the central bank maintains its slight appreciation path, the downward pressure on yields is likely to persist.

Investors will get their next update on 28 May, when the Ministry of Finance releases its mid-year fiscal review. The DMO will publish its next issuance schedule on 15 June. Both events are expected to confirm the current trajectory, but in a market this sensitive to supply and currency signals, nothing is guaranteed.
